name: dbdiagram.io
license: Proprietary service (the DBML language, parser and CLI are Apache 2.0)
summary: A web tool that draws entity-relationship diagrams from a schema you type in DBML, an open text language, and converts between DBML and SQL for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle.
intro: dbdiagram.io draws database diagrams from code. You type tables, columns, enums and references in DBML (Database Markup Language) in an editor on the left, and the diagram on the right updates as you type; you can also draw a reference by dragging between two fields. DBML is small and database-agnostic: `Table` blocks with columns and settings such as `[primary key]` or `[note: ...]`, `Enum` blocks, reusable `TablePartial` blocks, sample `records`, and `Ref:` lines such as `posts.user_id > users.id` for a many-to-one relationship. Diagrams export as images and PDFs, and as `CREATE TABLE` statements.

DBML is open source, and its CLI and the `@dbml/core` npm package do the conversions outside the website: `sql2dbml` reads PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake or Oracle DDL, `dbml2sql` writes PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or Oracle, and `db2dbml` reads the schema straight from a live PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery or Oracle database. That makes the diagram something you can regenerate in CI and keep in Git. The same maker’s dbdocs.io turns DBML into a documentation site.

The website is free for up to 10 diagrams. Personal Pro ($8 a month) adds unlimited diagrams, version history and an AI assistant that turns plain-language requests into DBML changes shown in a diff, with a monthly token quota. Team costs $75 a month for three editors and $5 for each extra editor.
strengths: Typing is faster than drawing, and a text schema can be diffed, reviewed and kept with the code
The language and converters are open source, so you aren’t locked into the website
Converts in both directions between DBML and the main SQL dialects, and can read a schema from a live database
A free plan that covers most personal use
limits: DBML covers tables, columns, references, indexes, enums and sample records; its documentation doesn’t cover views, triggers or functions, so it isn’t a full copy of a database’s schema
The diagram is a separate document: unless you regenerate it with `db2dbml`, it drifts from the real database
Version history, unlimited diagrams and the AI assistant need a paid plan
The editor is a hosted service; only the language and its tools are open source

story: Holistics, a Singapore-based business intelligence company, started building a diagram tool in August 2018. It began as a feature that interns built so Holistics customers could see their database schemas, and the team decided to release it on its own. Anthony Thong Do announced dbdiagram.io on October 22, 2018, as a quick database designer for analysts and developers, built on one idea: relying on a mouse to create tables and fields slows people down, so you type and the diagram follows.

About a year later users had made over 100,000 diagrams. Holistics turned the tool’s syntax into DBML, an open-source language with its own parser and converters, maintained on GitHub, and used it for dbdocs.io as well. By February 2025, 2.5 million DBML documents had been created through dbdiagram.io and dbdocs.io, by 1.4 million users. Later additions include `db2dbml` to read schemas from live databases, a VS Code extension and an AI assistant.

choices.choice: Write the schema as text, not draw it
choices.why: Analysts and developers work faster at a keyboard, and a text schema can be shared, versioned and converted.

choices.choice: Open the language separately from the app
choices.why: Publishing DBML with a parser and SQL converters let other tools read and write it, and lets users leave the website without losing their schemas.
One file can describe a schema and generate DDL for several databases, at the cost of leaving out features specific to one of them.
